newsitem.title: MEXICO: Two Mexicans near death in hunger strike over jobs.
newsitem.headline: Two Mexicans near death in hunger strike over jobs.

text.p: Two dismissed Mexican streetsweepers slipped dangerously close to death on Tuesday on the 85th day of a hunger strike that has become a major embarrassment for President Ernesto Zedillo's government.

The life-or-death protest in Mexico City, on behalf of 300 fired cleaners, cast a spotlight on the miserable conditions some government workers are forced to endure, as well as Mexico's dire joblessness.

Lying virtually unconscious under a plastic tarpaulin outside the National Human Rights Commission, Jorge Luis Alamilla and Venancio Jimenez could not talk and could barely open their eyes. Reporters on Tuesday were only permitted a brief glimpse of the two men inside their dark shelter.

Concerned doctors, forbidden by the protesters from treating their colleagues, said the two men may have sustained irreversible physical and mental damage from spending almost three months consuming only water, honey and glucose.
Mexican newspapers said the two men could die at any time.

"Doctor Ernesto Zedillo, the solution to the problem of the Tabasco cleaners ... is now in your hands alone," a group of 150 politicians and concerned citizens said in a manifesto published in Mexican newspapers on Tuesday.
It accused state officials of turning a blind eye to the men, who it said were just fighting for the right to work.

The two humble cleaners from Villahermosa, capital of the southeastern state of Tabasco, were among 300 fired by the city council last year. They said they were dismissed for refusing to do unpaid, off-duty jobs for local and state officials.
"There came a day when we simply refused to clean cars, wash dogs, tend gardens and take orders in the mansions of public servants," Jose Luis Montero, a spokesman for the protesters, told Reuters.

The protest gained extra force because Tabasco state governor Robert Madrazo -- the man who must authorise any solution -- was already a controversial figure. Opposition politicians accused him of spending more than 10 times the legal limit on his 1994 campaign to win election.

On Nov. 25 another five men joined the hunger strike, and on Tuesday they also looked frail and sickly. Earlier in their protest the men squirted syringefuls of their own blood at the walls of the Senate to draw attention.
Last weekend, on orders from Zedillo, the Interior Ministry began urgent negotiations to try to end the hunger strike.

Villahermosa officials told national radio on Tuesday they were offering to re-employ 200 of the municipal workers and pay extra severance to the 100 remaining. But the protesters appeared to be holding out for full reemployment.
"It looks like even the death of our stricken colleagues will not stir the authorities," said Rodrigo Gonzalez, father of three, who has been on hunger strike for 43 days.
"We will not get up until they give us our jobs back. That's the only way we can support our children and families."
More than a million Mexicans lost their jobs after Zedillo devalued the peso in December 1994, plunging Mexico into its worst slump in 50 years.
